title: Otis Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Otis wells have a 280-foot median depth, with drilling and completed-well costs estimated from local ground conditions.
h1: Wells and Water in Otis, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land near Otis means understanding both the well record and the ground beneath the lot. Within 5 miles of Otis, Colorado, DWR records show 249 permitted wells, with 100 recorded as constructed. Of those records, 117 report total depth, 46 report pump yield, and 13 report static water level.

The local numbers point to moderately deep wells with generally useful reported production, but the records are not a guarantee for a particular parcel. A neighboring well can help set expectations, while the permit, aquifer, construction details, and a proper water test matter for the final decision.

sections.heading: Otis well depth follows the plains geology
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Otis is 280 feet. The middle half runs from 235 to 316 feet, and the deepest well on record reaches 500 feet. The depth mix is fairly concentrated: 65% of reported wells are between 100 and 300 feet, while 35% fall between 300 and 600 feet. None are recorded under 100 feet or above 600 feet.

For a drilling bid, that median is a planning point, not a promised completion depth. A contractor may need to go deeper if the first water-bearing zone is inadequate or if casing and grout requirements change the design. Otis records name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers on 152 wells, the Ogallala on 95, and the High Plains Aquifer on 3. That mix supports checking nearby completions instead of relying on a countywide average.

sections.heading: Reported well yield is usually workable near Otis
sections.html:
Among the 46 Otis-area wells that report pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 10.0 to 24.8 gallons per minute. Reported production is not evenly spread at the low end: 65% show more than 15 gallons per minute, 28% fall from 5 to 15, and 7% fall from 1 to 5. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures describe tested or reported well performance, not the amount a household should pump continuously. A domestic permit may have different limits and conditions than a stock or irrigation well. DWR permit records show use categories of domestic or household at 43%, stock at 37%, irrigation at 34%, and monitoring at 3%. Ask for the well construction report, pump test, and permitted use before sizing a pump or planning irrigation.

sections.heading: Otis water levels are deep, but the trend is unclear
sections.html:
Only 13 wells in the local records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. Within that group, the median depth to water is 228 feet, with the middle half from 200 to 255 feet. That is useful for estimating pump lift and electrical needs, but it is not enough to establish a reliable local water-table trend.

The permit history does not substitute for water-level monitoring. Permits were issued in several decades, including 33 in the 1970s, 36 in the 1990s, 37 in the 2000s, 19 in the 2010s, and 10 in the 2020s; the newest permit year is 2025. Those counts show ongoing development, not a measured rise or decline in groundwater. For a parcel with an existing well, compare older and newer static measurements when available.

sections.heading: Permit history points to several established drillers
sections.html:
Otis has a long well-permit record, with permits dating back to the 1950s and a newest permit year of 2025. The records list 249 permitted wells within the local search area, although only 100 are recorded as constructed. That distinction matters: a permit map is not the same as a map of working, completed wells.

The most active named drillers in these records are Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc, associated with Twiss, Raymond L., with 35 records; Burgess Well Company Inc., associated with Burgess, Larry, with 21; and Schaal Drilling Co., associated with Schaal, Ruben T., with 13. Treat that history as a starting point. Confirm current licensing, availability, references, and what each bid includes before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: What a new Otis well may cost
sections.html:
For Otis ground described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the 280-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $9,800 to $15,400. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $15,800 to $27,400. Actual bids can move outside that range when access, casing, grout, difficult drilling, water treatment, or power work changes the scope. Ask for a written breakdown of drilling, casing, development, pump testing, pump equipment, tank, trenching, electrical, permits, and startup. A lower per-foot price may not be the lower total project cost.

sections.heading: Check water quality, yield, septic, and building limits
sections.html:
Three PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about 10 miles of Otis. There are no historic mine features in that mapped search and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These records do not prove contamination at a particular well, but they are a reason to test existing or new well water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby site history.

Low yield and a dry hole remain site-specific risks even when local reported yields look favorable. Confirm the permit type, aquifer, construction, static level, and pump test. A septic system also needs suitable soil, separation from the well, and enough usable space; its design can affect where a home, driveway, and outbuildings fit. Have the well and septic locations reviewed together before finalizing a building plan.

sections.heading: Use nearby wells before committing to an Otis lot
sections.html:
For a purchase or new build, begin with the exact parcel and then compare nearby records in Otis, Yuma, Akron, Eckley, Merino, Hillrose, and Atwood. The closest comparable wells are more useful than a broad regional assumption, especially where permits name both Ogallala and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers.

Request every available well permit, construction report, pump-yield result, static water-level reading, and water-quality test. Have a driller review whether a 280-foot planning depth and a 15.0-gallon-per-minute reported median fit the site, then price the complete system rather than the hole alone. If the property has no well, confirm water-rights and permit requirements with Colorado DWR before construction. For an existing home, make the offer contingent on satisfactory well flow, water quality, septic evaluation, and inspection of the pump and pressure equipment.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Otis, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Otis is 280 feet. The middle half runs from 235 to 316 feet. About 65% of reported wells are between 100 and 300 feet, while 35% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 500 feet, so a specific lot may require a different depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Otis?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 280-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $9,800 to $15,400. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $15,800 to $27,400. Request a complete written scope before comparing bids.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Otis?
faq.a: Among 46 local wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 24.8 gallons per minute. Reported results show 65% above 15 gallons per minute, 28% from 5 to 15, and 7% from 1 to 5. These records do not guarantee production at a new location.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Otis?
faq.a: The local map includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not establish contamination at a particular property. Test the well through a qualified laboratory before drinking, and review the well construction, nearby land uses, treatment needs, and any prior water-quality results.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a home on a well near Otis?
faq.a: Obtain the DWR permit and construction report, then verify the pump test, static water level, well yield, water quality, and permitted use. Only 13 local records report static water level, so measurements from the specific well matter. Also inspect the septic system and confirm that the well, septic, house, driveway, and planned improvements fit the lot.
